title: Very Precise Information
author: Marcus Luther
summary: High school English teacher Marcus Luther, listening to the new season of Sold a Story, reads Zig Engelmann's line that controlled instruction yields "very precise information about the learner" and feels that much of the discourse describes classrooms unlike most real ones. To show the gap he narrates a single fictional but composite lesson from fifteen years of teaching: students drifting in late, bathroom pass requests, an office aide at the door, and a reading of a Desmond Tutu speech that falls flat until he abandons the planned question and asks whether the woman should forgive. The room comes alive, yet the scripted exit ticket stays and the moment passes. Luther says this daily straddling between required curriculum and the room in front of you is the grey area most teachers work within, exhausting but also the beauty of the job. He argues that talk of objectivity and data-driven decisions sounds easy when one understands classrooms mostly through spreadsheets, and that decision-makers are far from classrooms affected by their decisions.
points: A narrated lesson shows the constant interruptions, such as tardies and passes, that make idealised instruction hard to run as scripted.
The core tension is between required standards and texts and the real-time conditions of the room, which teachers resolve by moment-to-moment choices.
Dropping the planned question for a simple yes-or-no on forgiveness produced the most engaged discussion of the day.
Luther is honest that he did not trust his instinct to scrap the exit ticket, and that the road not taken still nags at him.
His charge is that "precise information" and data-driven language can be fantasy for people who see classrooms only through spreadsheets.
quotes: While trying to continue wearing a “learner hat” about the current season of Emily Hanford’s Sold a Story, I recently decided to look into a bit more of Zig Engelmann’s writings other day.

You roll your eyes (it’s always this same student!) and close the door behind them. You direct students to set up their new page in their spiral for the bellringer posted on the screen, and then go to enter the attendance on your computer.
Weren’t we just talking about that space shuttle exploding?” one student asks upon opening the textbook to the page of the new article.

Still, you hold that feeling of disconnect and disappointment against an acknowledgment that the students are still trying their best, even the student who had their head down but kept going once you checked in with them.
The momentum builds into the whole-class conversation, as now you not only are calling on students randomly but you’re seeing hands pop up on their own to respond.

Almost all get started and at least through their first piece of evidence and explanation—even those who did not appear to be that engaged with the reading earlier on. You aren’t sure what to make of this.

The argument goes, I guess, that if these students would have had consistent, successful Direct Instruction up until they stepped into my high school English classroom, then all that variation would not exist.
